title: Gurudongmar Lake: altitude sickness and safety
meta_description: Gurudongmar Lake is at 5,430 m. Who should not go, how to acclimatise in Lachen, the warning signs of altitude sickness and what to do if someone gets ill.
summary: Gurudongmar Lake sits at 5,430 m, and most visitors climb there from Lachen at about 2,750 m in a single morning. Healthy adults usually manage with care: a night in Lachen, water, no alcohol, slow walking and 20–30 minutes at the shore. Children under five and people with heart or lung disease should not go.

sections.heading: Why Gurudongmar is a different kind of day
paras: Most of North Sikkim's sights are high but forgiving. Lachung is about 2,700 m and Yumthang 3,564 m, heights most people feel only as a little breathlessness on the stairs. Gurudongmar is another matter. The Government of Sikkim gives its height as 5,430 m, which places it among the highest lakes in the world that tourists can drive to. At that height the air pressure is roughly half of what it is at sea level, so every breath carries about half the oxygen you are used to.

The problem is speed. The standard plan leaves Lachen at about 4 am and reaches the lake by 8–10 am, a climb of about 2,700 m in four or five hours. Mountain medicine guidance suggests that above 3,000 m you should raise your sleeping height by no more than 300–500 m a day. A day trip that returns to sleep lower is safer than sleeping high, which is why you never stay the night near the lake, but the body still feels the jump. Plan for it rather than hope for the best.

sections.heading: How altitude sickness shows up
paras: Altitude sickness comes in three forms. The common one is acute mountain sickness, or AMS: headache plus one or more of nausea, poor appetite, dizziness, tiredness and poor sleep. Many visitors to Gurudongmar feel a mild version, and it usually eases as you go down. The two serious forms are rare on a short visit but can kill, and the signs are worth learning before you go.

The table below is a simple guide, not a medical manual. The rule that matters most is this: symptoms that get worse as you go higher, or that do not improve with rest, mean going down at once. Do not wait for them to pass at the lake.

sections.heading: Who should not go
paras: Some travellers should skip the lake and enjoy Lachen, Thangu or the Lachung valley instead. There is no shame in it; Yumthang at 3,564 m is a fine day out. Operators usually will not take children under five. We also advise these groups to stay below Thangu, or to go only after a doctor's clear approval.
list: Children under five, who cannot tell you clearly how they feel.
Anyone with heart disease, a past heart attack, uncontrolled high blood pressure or a pacemaker issue.
Anyone with lung disease such as asthma that is not well controlled, COPD or a recent chest infection.
Pregnant travellers, and anyone with severe anaemia or sickle-cell disease.
Anyone with a cold, fever, diarrhoea or vomiting in the days before the trip.
Anyone who has had HAPE or HACE before.

sections.heading: Getting ready: acclimatise before the lake
paras: Good preparation starts in Gangtok. Spend at least one night there at about 1,650 m before the drive north, and do not arrive in Lachen on the same day you land at Bagdogra. In Lachen, at about 2,750 m, walk slowly, eat a light dinner, drink two to three litres of water through the day and skip alcohol and sleeping pills. Smokers should stop for these days if they can.

For seniors, anyone who has struggled with altitude before, or travellers who simply want a safer margin, add a second night in Lachen and spend the spare day on a gentle walk to Lachen Monastery, founded in 1858. That one extra night makes a real difference. Group packages rarely offer it, so you will need a private car or a custom booking.

Some doctors prescribe acetazolamide to help prevent AMS. It is a prescription medicine with side effects and is not right for everyone, including people allergic to sulpha drugs. Discuss it with your own doctor before the trip; do not buy it over the counter on a driver's advice.

sections.heading: On the day at the lake
paras: Leave Lachen at 4–5 am. Wear everything: thermal inners, a fleece, a down or padded jacket, a windproof shell, a woollen cap, gloves and two pairs of socks. Dawn temperatures on the plateau are well below freezing for much of the year, and the wind is the real enemy. Take a packed breakfast and a flask of warm water, filled from your hotel filter, because packaged water is banned in Lachen and above.

Stop at Thangu, about 3,900 m, for tea, toilets and the army check, and use the stop honestly. Ask everyone in the car how they feel. A child who has gone quiet or an adult who is unusually irritable may be feeling the height. If anyone has a severe headache or is vomiting, the car turns back here.

At the lake, move slowly, talk little and keep your visit to 20–30 minutes. Do not run, carry heavy bags or climb the slopes for a better photograph. The sun is fierce at 5,430 m, so wear sunglasses and sunscreen. Portable oxygen cans sold in Gangtok for ₹500–900, indicative 2026, give a few breaths of relief at most; they are not a treatment and must not delay going down.

sections.heading: What to pack for the Gurudongmar day
paras: Pack the night before in Lachen, because you will leave in the dark and half asleep. Keep one small bag on your lap in the car with everything you need for the lake, and leave the big luggage in the boot for the drive on to Lachung. Buy what you lack in Gangtok, where prices are lower than in Lachen or at the Thangu stalls.
list: Thermal inner top and leggings, a fleece and a down or padded jacket.
A windproof outer layer, a woollen cap that covers the ears, and warm gloves.
Two pairs of woollen socks and shoes with a good grip for icy patches.
Sunglasses, sunscreen and lip balm; the light is strong at 5,430 m.
A refillable bottle and a flask of warm water from your hotel filter.
Packed breakfast, dry fruit and chocolate for energy on the way.
Regular medicines, prescriptions, painkillers, anti-nausea tablets and oral rehydration salts.
Original photo ID for the checkposts and a little cash for tea at Thangu.
A plastic bag to carry all rubbish back down; nothing should be left at the lake.

sections.heading: If someone becomes ill
paras: The treatment for serious altitude sickness is descent, and descent works fast: dropping even 500–1,000 m often brings rapid relief. Tell the driver immediately and start down. Do not wait for the rest of the group to finish photographs. A private car makes this easier, which is one reason we suggest one for families with older members.

The Indian Army has medical posts in the area, including at Thangu, and soldiers have helped many tourists over the years. Beyond that, proper hospital care is in Mangan and Gangtok, many hours away. Carry your regular medicines and prescriptions, a basic first-aid kit and travel insurance that covers high-altitude sightseeing. Check current status before you travel, both for the road and for any new medical rules.

faqs.a: The Government of Sikkim gives the height as 5,430 m, about 17,800 feet, though some sources quote slightly different figures. It is among the highest lakes in the world that tourists can reach by road. Most visitors climb to it from Lachen, at about 2,750 m, in a single morning and return to sleep lower the same day.

faqs.q: Is Gurudongmar safe for senior citizens
faqs.a: Many healthy seniors visit safely, but the risk rises with age and health problems. Anyone with heart or lung disease or uncontrolled blood pressure should see a doctor first and may be advised not to go. Add a second night in Lachen to acclimatise, use a private car so you can turn back at any time, and keep the lake visit to 20–30 minutes.

faqs.q: Can children go to Gurudongmar Lake
faqs.a: Operators usually will not take children under five, and we agree: small children cannot explain symptoms and can become ill quickly at 5,430 m. Older children who are well, warm and drinking water usually manage a short visit. Watch for unusual quietness, crying, vomiting or drowsiness, and turn back at once if you see them.

faqs.q: What are the signs of altitude sickness at Gurudongmar
faqs.a: Headache, nausea, poor appetite, dizziness and tiredness are the common signs of mild acute mountain sickness. Danger signs are a severe headache that painkillers do not ease, repeated vomiting, confusion, stumbling, breathlessness at rest or a wet cough. Any danger sign means descending immediately and seeking medical help at Thangu or lower.

faqs.q: Should I take Diamox for Gurudongmar
faqs.a: Acetazolamide, sold as Diamox, can help prevent acute mountain sickness, but it is a prescription medicine with side effects and is unsuitable for some people, including those allergic to sulpha drugs. Ask your own doctor well before the trip. It is no substitute for a night in Lachen, steady water intake and a short stay at the lake.

faqs.q: Do oxygen cans help at Gurudongmar
faqs.a: Only a little. Portable oxygen cans sold in Gangtok for about ₹500–900, indicative 2026, hold a few minutes of oxygen and can ease breathlessness briefly. They do not treat altitude sickness. If someone has severe symptoms, the answer is to go down at once, not to keep spraying oxygen at the lake.

faqs.q: How long can I stay at Gurudongmar Lake
faqs.a: We advise 20–30 minutes at the shore, walking slowly. Army staff may also limit time at the lake. Longer stays increase the risk of symptoms without adding much to the experience. Take your photographs, offer a prayer if you wish and head back down to Thangu and Lachen, where most people feel better quickly.

faqs.q: How cold is it at Gurudongmar
faqs.a: Very cold for much of the year. Dawn temperatures on the plateau are well below freezing, and the wind makes it feel colder. The lake is usually frozen from about late November to April. Even in May and October you need thermals, a down or padded jacket, a windproof shell, a cap, gloves and warm socks.

faqs.q: Is there a hospital near Gurudongmar Lake
faqs.a: No. The Indian Army has medical posts in the area, including at Thangu, which have helped many tourists. Proper hospital care is in Mangan and Gangtok, several hours' drive away. That is why prevention matters: acclimatise in Lachen, turn back early if anyone is unwell and carry insurance that covers high-altitude sightseeing.
